title: Starting a massive open-source board game engine (Shogi, Go, Chess, Luzhanqi) coded entirely on my phone with AI! 📱♟️
author: APimpNamedChimp
selftext:
Hey everyone! I’m officially starting a new devlog journey and wanted to share the starting line.

My Background: I used to build in Unreal Engine back in the day—mostly handling assets, lighting setups, and working deeply with reality/eye reflections. I even built an entire virtual arcade system. I know how to make my own stuff manually, but honestly, now that AI tools are here, it makes prototyping so much faster and easier—especially for the crazy challenge I’m taking on.

The Challenge: I am doing 100% of the project management, file structuring, and coding directly on my mobile phone using a mobile code editor app and an AI assistant to help translate my ideas into code.

The Plan:

The Tech Stack: Pure HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript so it runs flawlessly on mobile browsers and can be installed as an offline app.

The Graphics: Outside of this AI-generated PNG splash logo, everything else will be pure, crisp SVG files for the board and pieces so it scales perfectly on any device.

The Roadmap: Step 1 is building a standard Shogi game. Step 2 is building 3 custom Shogi variants of my own design. If I get the framework working smoothly, I plan to expand this into a massive universal board game engine adding Chess, Go, and Luzhanqi.

I just wanted to share the logo I generated for the 2-second boot splash screen and state my intentions. The framework is completely open-source, and I'll be pushing everything to GitHub and Itch.io down the road.

Would love to connect with anyone else using web tech or coding on mobile!

comments.author: mallcopsarebastards
comments.body:
\> The Tech Stack: Pure HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript so it runs flawlessly on mobile browsers and can be installed as an offline app.

This is definitely a misunderstanding of the underlying technologies. Flawless cross browser portability is extremely difficult with pure html/css/javascript. This is one of the core reasons people use pre-existing frameworks. There are tons of subtle rendering differentials across browsers, even across versions of the same browser. Framework maintainers are putting in the work to bridge those.

replies.author: mallcopsarebastards
replies.body: use a framework that has already built a cross browser rendering engine. Otherwise you're trying to reinvent a wheel that has been iteratively built, tested, and fixed over probably decades.
